## Introduction

The human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is a neglected oncogenic retrovirus that primarily affects marginalized and isolated populations. Although transmission has been controlled in some developed regions, HTLV-1 remains disattended across much of the global south. @nishijima2019 @martin2018 The virus directly causes an aggressive form of T-cell lymphoma (ATLL, Adult T-cell Leukemia/Lymphoma) and is linked to several autoimmune disorders, particularly HAM/TSP. Even seemingly asymptomatic carriers face a significantly higher risk of death from indirect complications. @schierhout2020 @valcarcel2022 Compounding these disparities, HTLV-1 predominantly impacts rural populations with low genetic admixture—yet whether this divergence confers any deleterious effect remains unclear.

HTLV-1 exhibits remarkable genetic stability, with its proviral genome flanked by long terminal repeats (LTRs) containing highly variable U3 and U5 regions, followed by the *env* gene as the second most variable region. Current classification relies on *LTR* and *env* diversity, reflecting geographic distribution but not necessarily pathogenicity. Major functional differences have been proposed for Tax region (Tax A or Transcontinental, and Tax B Japanese) , and deffective viruses have been described as scape mechanisms to limit immunological function in the host during progression. While positive selection likely drives variability in these regions, the overall proviral stability suggests that minor genetic differences may still significantly impact viral behavior and disease outcomes. 

The main factors related to ATLL progression have been controversially validated in population from the global north, where some HLA has been demostrated to be protective and specific virus subtypes associated to HAM/TSP or ATLL, however the data is only based mainly in Japanese cohorts.

## Methods

### Population study and HTLV-1 confirmation

After informed consent, blood samples were collected from patients of the prospective HTLV-1 cohort at the Instituto de Medicina Tropical Alexander Von Humbold (Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, Lima-Peru). The study was approved by the Ethics committee of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, Miayazaki University and Kagoshima University. All patients were previously HTLV-1 screened and confirmed by an Enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay (ELISA, **details**), and PCR?/western-blot?.

### Methods
Recombination analyses

Recombination was initially evaluated using the phi-test followed by a exploratory screening using RDP, GENECONV, Bootscan, MaxChi, SisCan and 3Seq and LARD, implemented in RDP4.5. Potential recombination was suspected when at least four methods showed a Bonferroni-corrected P-value threshold of 0.05(or smaller). Sequences with potential recombination signal were evaluated with GARD, implemented in Hyphy, and  excluded from the final data set.
An exploratory screening for recombination was performed using phylogenetic methods (Bootscan and RDP), and nucleotide substitution methods (Chimaera, GENECONV, MaxChi, SisCan and 3Seq), Additionally phi-test performed in the RDP4.5 software. Sequences with potential recombination signal were considered when at least four alogorithms reached a threshold p-value of 0.05 with Bonferroni correction.

Following reads extraction from the chromosome 6, coverage and quality score analyses were performed for all HLA regions. High-resolution HLA typing was carried out using OptiType (2-field resolution for HLA-I) and HLA-LA (3-field resolution for HLA-I/II). Allotypes failing quality thresholds (score \<0.8 or average coverage \<20) were discarded. Results from both bioinformatics tools were pairwise compared, and considering the average coverage for HLA-II, only HLA-I was considered to further analysis. The concordances and Cohen's Kappa between HLA-LA and Optitype were 93%, 85%, and 100% for HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C, respectively. The HLA-LA pipeline was selected for further analyses.Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium (HWE) was tested for each locus using the exact test implemented on the pegas package with 1000 replicates with a significance threshold of α=0.05. Pairwise F<sub>ST</sub> was estimated using Weir & Cockerham’s (1984) method with 10,000 bootstrap replicates implemented on the package hierfstat. Significant differentiation was inferred when 95% CIs excluded zero.

HLA class I allele frequencies were calculated after reduction to 2-field resolution using the *reduceHlaCalls* function from the package midasHLA. Frequencies for the Peruvian population were obtained using the function *getHlaFrequencies* and compared to the USA National Marrow Donor Program (NMDP) populations that were retrieved from Allele Frequency Net Database (http://www.allelefrequencies.net/).

# Results

A total of 67 patients with confirmed HTLV-1 infection were included in the study, comprising 10 HAM/TSP patients and 57 asymptomatic carriers (ACs). The lifetime *Strongyloides* infection rate was 56.7% overall and more frequent among males. No association was found between *Strongyloides* infection and HTLV-1-related complications. Demographic and epidemiological characteristics are detailed in **Table 1**. During the 5-year follow-up, the progression rate to ATL among ACs was 5.3% (3 cases). Notably, the 5-year mortality rate was 15%, although 12% of patients were lost to follow-up during COVID-19 pandemic.

A total of 71 DNA samples—corresponding to 67 patients (including 4 serial samples)—were analyzed. The median HTLV-1 genome coverage in the Peruvian cohort was 158x (IQR: 23-218); (**Supplementary Figure 1**). After excluding 4 samples with less than 5x coverage, the final dataset comprised 63 cases (**Supplementary Figure 2**). Among these, 3 cases (4.8%) harbored type II defective viruses (5’LTR-deleted; **Figure 1A**). Notably, 2 out 3 ATL cases and 1 AC exhibited these deletions. No type I defective viruses were detected in this cohort.

HLA-I allele frequencies

The Peruvian HTLV-1 cohort exhibited distinct HLA-I allele distributions, with A*02:01 being the most frequent allele at the HLA-A locus (44%), followed by A*24:02 (17%) and A*68:01 (7%). The HLA-B locus showed equal frequencies for B*35:01 and B*35:05 (12% each), with B*48:01 at 11%, while the HLA-C locus was dominated by C*04:01 (29%), followed by C*01:02 (18%) and C\*07:02 (13%). Comparative analyses with the NMDP database and a Japanese HTLV-1 cohort revealed population-specific variations, with HLA-A and HLA-C conforming to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (p=0.06 and p=0.33, respectively), but HLA-B showing significant deviation (p=0.01), likely reflecting its well-documented role in balancing selection or cohort-specific demographic factors. Complete allele frequencies are detailed in Supplementary Table 1. The Peruvian and Japanese cohorts showed significant moderate genetic differentiation (mean F<sub>ST</sub> = 0.047, 95% CI \[0.023, 0.072\]), consistent with population-specific HLA allele frequency distributions.
